notes.opus_reason: This is Elon Musk speaking, not Dwarkesh, and he says it while describing the solar cells SpaceX and Tesla intend to build themselves at 100 gigawatts a year, 'from raw materials to finish the cell'. So the claim is about a cell he plans to make, while the note answers with the price of today's specialist space cells. Those two numbers are real: the Polytechnique Insights article does say 300 euros per watt against 10 to 20 cents, and the Christian Science Monitor does report the NASA 12-to-80-times figure. But the NASA figure covers a whole space solar power system including launch, not the cost of making a cell, so it does not speak to what Musk said. The note's other assertion, that space cells need radiation-shielding cover glass, is not in either source, and the Polytechnique article in fact says the gap is narrowing because satellite constellations are switching to modified terrestrial cells, which is close to Musk's own argument. The underlying point is worth making, because a listener would otherwise believe space cells are cheaper today when they are not, but as written the note does not cleanly meet the claim.

The National WWII Museum interview with Michael Neufeld, the historian who wrote the standard von Braun biography, says he was arrested by the Gestapo in March 1944 over drunken party remarks that Germany would lose the war and that the real task was a spaceship, and that he was rescued by Dornberger and Speer. My own searching confirms a two-week detention in a Stettin cell and turns up no death sentence and no halted execution anywhere. The gap is large: a listener comes away believing the Nazis were about to execute their best rocket engineer for refusing weapons work, when the record shows a two-week arrest for defeatism that ended through intervention. Dwarkesh is not the speaker here, but he does not dispute the facts of the story, and a clean historical correction on his video is the sort of thing he is likely to take well.

notes.opus_reason: The fact is right. Naomi Whitehead was born on 26 September 1910, became the oldest living person in the United States after Elizabeth Francis died in October 2024, and turned 115 in September 2025, so in February 2026 she was 115 years and about four months old, not 114. It also bears on the sentence that follows, where Musk says it is safe to assume anyone recorded as 115 and alive is a typo or dead, since the oldest living American was in fact 115. What gives me pause is size: this is a one-year slip on a passing number inside a three-hour interview, and the wider argument, that the Social Security files list people far beyond any real human age, is untouched by it. Nathan should decide whether a note this small is worth spending on Dwarkesh, especially as the speaker is Musk rather than him.

notes.opus_reason: There is a real error here. The 2023 Social Security inspector general audit found 18.9 million numberholders born in 1920 or earlier with no death information on the Numident, and the roughly 21 million figure Musk posted in 2025 covered everyone over 99, so neither number describes people over 115, and neither describes anyone as confirmed alive. The note's sources support this and the 44,000 payment figure. My hesitation is about how it is written. The sharpest correction, that the figure covers people aged 100 and up rather than 115 and up, is left for the reader to work out from 'born before 1920', and half the note is spent on benefits, which is the same off-target ground as the duplicate note on this sentence and which Musk himself qualifies moments later when Dwarkesh asks whether those people were getting paid. Rewritten to lead with the age range, this would be a strong note.
